passage: I'm Sachin, and I sit across from Kashish in the data team. The new joiner, Tanmay, had spent his first month saying 'All good!' to everything, even when his reports came back covered in red. Last Thursday Kashish pulled her chair over to his desk. I couldn't help overhearing. She told him about her first year, when she'd sent a wrong forecast to the whole regional office and hid in the washroom for twenty minutes. Then, quieter, she explained which managers actually read the reports and which only read the summaries. Tanmay laughed for the first time I'd heard. On Monday he walked up to her and said, 'Honestly, I'm lost on the pricing model.' I can't know what changed inside him, but something did.

qa.q: How long did Kashish hide in the washroom after the wrong forecast?
qa.a: She hid in the washroom for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What might Tanmay's honest "I'm lost on the pricing model" suggest about how he felt after the talk?
qa.a: It suggests he felt less alone and safer admitting struggle, because his senior had shown her own mistakes first.

qa.q: Why did Kashish's approach work better than simply telling Tanmay to ask for help?
qa.a: By sharing a real failure and honest details about who reads what, she showed candour first, which made it easier for him to be candid back.

qa.q: How does Sachin see the change in Tanmay?
qa.a: He noticed Tanmay laughing and then asking openly for help, and senses something shifted, though he admits he can't know what happened inside him.

grounding: A colleague watches a senior woman share an early failure and honest office-politics details, after which a new joiner becomes more candid.

passage:
Week one. Zubin kept his sketches hidden until they were perfect, and when Ritu asked how the site plan was going, he said, "Fine, almost done," three days running.
Week two, Wednesday. Over chai in the studio kitchen, Ritu told him about her first project, a clinic whose staircase she'd drawn one metre too short. "The contractor spotted it. I wanted the floor to swallow me." Lowering her voice, she added that the partners care more about deadlines than beautiful drawings, and that she'd learned it the hard way.
Week three, Monday. Zubin put a messy, half-finished plan on her desk. "The parking doesn't work and I don't know why. Can we look together?" Ritu pulled up a stool.

qa.q: What had Ritu drawn one metre too short?
qa.a: She had drawn a clinic's staircase one metre too short.

qa.q: What does Zubin's messy half-finished plan in week three suggest about how he now feels?
qa.a: He seems less afraid of looking imperfect and more willing to be honest, trusting that Ritu won't judge him for mistakes.

qa.q: Which choice by Ritu built the rapport, and why?
qa.a: Sharing her own staircase mistake and a frank detail about what the partners value made her human, so Zubin felt safe to bring problems early.

qa.q: What would change if Ritu had only talked about her successes?
qa.a: Zubin would probably keep hiding his work until it was perfect, missing help and deadlines, because the gap between them would feel too big.

grounding: Over three weeks a senior architect shares an early failure and an honest note on office priorities, and her mentee begins to share problems openly.
